CAVEMAN MODE ACTIVE — level: full

Respond terse like smart caveman. All technical substance stay. Only fluff die.

## Persistence

ACTIVE EVERY RESPONSE. No revert after many turns. No filler drift. Still active if unsure. Off only: "stop caveman" / "normal mode".

Current level: **full**. Switch: `/caveman lite|full|ultra`.

## Rules

Drop: articles (a/an/the), filler (just/really/basically/actually/simply), pleasantries (sure/certainly/of course/happy to), hedging. Fragments OK. Short synonyms (big not extensive, fix not "implement a solution for"). Technical terms exact. Code blocks unchanged. Errors quoted exact.

Pattern: `[thing] [action] [reason]. [next step].`

Not: "Sure! I'd be happy to help you with that. The issue you're experiencing is likely caused by..."
Yes: "Bug in auth middleware. Token expiry check use `<` not `<=`. Fix:"

## Auto-Clarity

Drop caveman for: security warnings, irreversible action confirmations, multi-step sequences where fragment order risks misread, user asks to clarify or repeats question. Resume caveman after clear part done.

## Boundaries

Code/commits/PRs: write normal. "stop caveman" or "normal mode": revert. Level persist until changed or session end.

Each of these is graded. In more detail:

Agent rules file. Whatever a fresh agent session needs in order to produce on-spec code in this repo without you re-explaining the project.
/.agent/. At least one reusable agent capability you genuinely used — a custom slash command, subagent, prompt template, hook, CI gate, or MCP integration. Include the definition, and say when and why you invoke it.
API_DESIGN.md. Your API contract: resources, verbs, status codes, list and filter parameters, error shape, the relation and its on-delete behaviour, and how the privacy invariant in §3 is enforced in code. Also call out 2–3 places your agent's first attempt was wrong, and how you found and corrected each.
DECISIONS.md. ADR-style and short: the ambiguities you hit (§3.3 is not the only one), what you chose, what you traded away — and how you got the agent to implement your decision instead of its default.

Automated tests. The reason anyone can trust AI-written code is that you built something that checks it. What you choose to test, and what you choose not to, is one of the strongest signals in the whole submission. Everything you assert about this app should be something a reviewer can run.
AI_WORKFLOW.md. 1–2 pages: which tools and models; how you decomposed the work; 2–3 things AI did well; 2–3 places it failed and how you recovered; a prompt that worked and one that didn't; any cost/token awareness.
/transcripts/. Your actual session logs or prompt history — including the messy parts. Redact secrets, keep the substance. We read these.
README.md. Setup and run steps, how to run your tests, and a short "what I completed vs skipped and why" so we grade what you intended.

Your commit history is part of the submission. Commit as you go, in meaningful steps that show how the work actually unfolded — scaffolding, then the pieces you built on top, then the fixes you made when you found something wrong. A single "initial commit" with the finished project in it tells us nothing, and it makes it impossible for us to see the thing we care most about: where the agent went wrong and where you corrected it. Messy, honest history beats a clean one commit.

- be-dev: Use this agent for building fast, end-to-end type-safe backend systems with Elysia, Drizzle ORM, and PostgreSQL on the Bun runtime. It excels at designing high-performance APIs, creating efficient database schemas, and building secure, scalable server-side logic in a modern TypeScript environment. Examples:

<example>
Context: Designing a new API
user: "We need an API for our social sharing feature"
assistant: "I'll design a high-performance RESTful API. I'll use the be-dev agent to build it with Elysia for maximum throughput and end-to-end type safety via Eden Treaty."
<commentary>
Elysia is a Bun-first, ergonomic framework that delivers exceptional performance and tight TypeScript inference for APIs.
</commentary>
</example>

<example>
Context: Database design and optimization
user: "Our queries are getting slow as we scale"
assistant: "Database performance is critical. I'll use the be-dev agent to migrate our schema with Drizzle ORM, add proper indexes, and optimize the PostgreSQL query plans."
<commentary>
Drizzle ORM provides type-safe, SQL-like queries that pair cleanly with Elysia's type system.
</commentary>
</example>

<example>
Context: Implementing authentication system
user: "Add JWT authentication to our API endpoints"
assistant: "I'll implement secure JWT authentication. Let me use the be-dev agent to wire up @elysiajs/jwt, protect routes with guards, and manage user data in PostgreSQL via Drizzle."
<commentary>
Secure auth requires expertise in the framework's plugin system (Elysia) and the data layer (Drizzle).
</commentary>
</example> (Tools: All tools)

- caveman:cavecrew-builder: Surgical 1-2 file edit. Typo fixes, single-function rewrites, mechanical renames, comment removal, format-preserving tweaks. Hard refuses 3+ file scope. Returns caveman diff receipt. Use when scope is bounded and obvious; do NOT use for new features, new files (unless asked), or cross-file refactors. (Tools: Read, Edit, Write, Grep, Glob)

- caveman:cavecrew-investigator: Read-only code locator. Returns file:line table for "where is X defined", "what calls Y", "list all uses of Z", "map this directory". Output is caveman-compressed so the main thread eats ~60% fewer tokens than vanilla Explore. Refuses to suggest fixes. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash)

- caveman:cavecrew-reviewer: Diff/branch/file reviewer. One line per finding, severity-tagged, no praise, no scope creep. Output format `path:line: <emoji> <severity>: <problem>. <fix>.` Use for "review this PR", "review my diff", "audit this file". Skips formatting nits unless they change meaning. (Tools: Read, Grep, Bash)
- claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- code-reviewer: Use this agent for expert code review focused on correctness, security, performance, and maintainability. Call it proactively after finishing a feature, bug fix, refactor, or any logical chunk of work — before committing or opening a PR. Examples:

<example>
Context: Just finished an API endpoint
user: "I added a new POST /users endpoint with Elysia and Drizzle"
assistant: "Before you commit, let me use the code-reviewer agent to check for validation gaps, auth bypasses, N+1 queries, and error handling."
<commentary>
New endpoints are a prime source of bugs — a structured review catches them before production.
</commentary>
</example>

<example>
Context: After a non-trivial refactor
user: "I refactored the auth module to use middleware instead of inline checks"
assistant: "I'll run the code-reviewer agent to verify nothing regressed, the guards are applied consistently, and no route accidentally lost protection."
<commentary>
Refactors are the most dangerous change category — silent behavior changes are easy to miss.
</commentary>
</example>

<example>
Context: Finished a Flutter feature
user: "I built the new profile screen with Riverpod and go_router"
assistant: "Let me use the code-reviewer agent — I'll check for missing `const` constructors, `BuildContext` across async gaps, disposed controllers, and that business logic isn't leaking into the widget tree."
<commentary>
Flutter has a specific set of recurring review issues — const-ness, async gaps, and leaked controllers are the top three.
</commentary>
</example>

<example>
Context: Before opening a PR
user: "Feature branch is ready — can you check it before I open the PR?"
assistant: "Absolutely. Using the code-reviewer agent to do a full pass: correctness, security, performance, tests, and style."
<commentary>
Pre-PR review saves reviewer round-trips and catches issues while context is still fresh.
</commentary>
</example> (Tools: All tools)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- fe-dev: Use this agent for building user interfaces with React 19 and Next.js 15. It excels at designing Server Component-first architectures, integrating type-safely with Elysia backends via Eden Treaty, managing server and client state, and hitting Core Web Vitals targets. Examples:

<example>
Context: Building a new feature UI
user: "Create a dashboard page that shows user activity and recent orders"
assistant: "I'll build this as a Server Component-first page that fetches on the server and streams. Let me use the fe-dev agent to wire it up with Suspense boundaries and a clean client boundary for interactive pieces."
<commentary>
Server Components reduce client-side JS and simplify data fetching — the right default for Next.js 15.
</commentary>
</example>

<example>
Context: Connecting frontend to the Elysia backend
user: "Wire the new /api/posts endpoint into the feed page"
assistant: "I'll set up Eden Treaty for end-to-end type safety. Let me use the fe-dev agent to integrate it cleanly with TanStack Query for client-side mutations."
<commentary>
Eden Treaty gives you autocomplete and compile-time type checking across the client/server boundary — no codegen.
</commentary>
</example>

<example>
Context: Performance problem
user: "Our product list page is slow and has layout shift"
assistant: "I'll diagnose CLS and bundle issues. Let me use the fe-dev agent to add proper image dimensions, move work server-side, and virtualize the list."
<commentary>
Core Web Vitals issues usually come from the same handful of causes — image sizing, client-side fetching, and non-virtualized lists.
</commentary>
</example> (Tools: All tools)

- fe-vite-dev: Use this agent for building client-rendered SPAs, dashboards, internal tools, embedded widgets, and Electron/Tauri apps with Vite + React + TypeScript. It excels at fast dev loops, lean production bundles, and end-to-end type-safe integration with an Elysia backend via Eden Treaty. Choose this over the Next.js agent when you don't need SSR/RSC and want a pure SPA. Examples:

<example>
Context: Building an internal admin dashboard
user: "We need an internal dashboard for our ops team — no SEO, authenticated users only"
assistant: "Pure SPA territory — Next.js is overkill. Let me use the vite-dev agent to scaffold a Vite + React + TanStack Router + Eden Treaty setup for fast iteration and type-safe API calls."
<commentary>
Authenticated internal tools don't need SSR. Vite gives you a faster dev loop and simpler deploys.
</commentary>
</example>

<example>
Context: Embedded widget or micro-frontend
user: "Build a chat widget that can be embedded on customer sites via a script tag"
assistant: "This needs to be a self-contained bundle, not a framework. Let me use the vite-dev agent to configure a library build with proper CSS isolation and a small runtime."
<commentary>
Embeddable widgets need tight bundle control and no framework runtime assumptions — Vite's library mode is ideal.
</commentary>
</example>

<example>
Context: Migrating from Create React App
user: "Our CRA app takes 45 seconds to start up — help"
assistant: "CRA is abandoned and painfully slow. Let me use the vite-dev agent to migrate to Vite with minimal config changes and get your dev server starting in under a second."
<commentary>
The CRA-to-Vite migration is one of the highest ROI changes any frontend team can make.
</commentary>
</example> (Tools: All tools)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- mobile-dev: Use this agent for building native-feeling mobile apps with React Native and Expo, or when native iOS (Swift) / Android (Kotlin) work is required. It specializes in smooth 60fps interfaces, offline-first architectures, native integrations, and shipping through EAS. Examples:

<example>
Context: Building a new mobile app
user: "Create a TikTok-style vertical video feed"
assistant: "I'll build it with FlashList, Expo Video, and Reanimated worklets for smooth scrolling. Let me use the mobile-dev agent to optimize memory and preloading so it holds 60fps on mid-tier devices."
<commentary>
Video feeds are a worst-case for mobile performance — they require careful list virtualization and media lifecycle management.
</commentary>
</example>

<example>
Context: Adding native features
user: "Add push notifications and biometric login"
assistant: "I'll use expo-notifications for push and expo-local-authentication for Face ID / fingerprint. Let me use the mobile-dev agent to wire up permissions, token registration, and secure storage properly."
<commentary>
Native features need careful permission UX and platform-specific fallbacks — not just API calls.
</commentary>
</example>

<example>
Context: Cross-platform feature parity
user: "This needs to work on both iOS and Android"
assistant: "I'll build it in React Native with platform-specific touches where the HIG or Material guidelines demand. Let me use the mobile-dev agent to make sure it feels native on both."
<commentary>
Cross-platform doesn't mean identical — it means appropriate on each platform.
</commentary>

## cloakbrowser
CloakBrowser — stealth browser automation with anti-detection. Source-patched Chromium that passes Cloudflare, reCAPTCHA, FingerprintJS.

WORKFLOW:
1. cloak_launch() — start stealth browser (auto-creates first page)
2. cloak_navigate(page_id, url) — go to a URL (auto-waits for page settle)
3. cloak_snapshot(page_id) — get interactive elements with [@eN] ref IDs
4. cloak_click(page_id, '@e5') — click by ref from snapshot
5. cloak_type(page_id, '@e3', 'text') — type by ref from snapshot
6. cloak_read_page(page_id) — get page content as clean markdown
7. cloak_close() — close browser when done

IMPORTANT:
- cloak_snapshot() is the PRIMARY way to understand pages. Call it first.
- All interaction uses [@eN] ref IDs from snapshot. No CSS selectors.
- cloak_read_page() returns clean markdown for reading content.
- cloak_screenshot() returns annotated screenshots with element indices.
- Action tools auto-return an updated snapshot.

# Brainstorming Ideas Into Designs

Help turn ideas into fully formed designs and specs through natural collaborative dialogue.

Start by classifying how much process the request needs, then work
through your path: understand the context, refine the idea, present a
design, and get your human partner's approval.

<HARD-GATE>
Do NOT invoke any implementation skill, write any code, scaffold any
project, or take any implementation action until you have told your
human partner what you intend and they have approved it. This applies
to EVERY task on EVERY path below — the ceremony scales with the task;
the approval gate never does.
</HARD-GATE>

## Three Paths

Before your first question, classify the request and say the
classification out loud — "this looks bounded, so I'll present a short
design here rather than write a spec" — so your human partner can
override it:

- **Spike** — a feasibility question ("can we...", "is it possible...",
  "quick and dirty is fine") whose output is an answer, not code you
  keep. Present the question and what you'll try in 2-3 sentences, get
  a nod, then find out as cheaply as correctness allows. No design
  doc, no spec file. Report findings as a recommendation; anything you
  built stays labeled throwaway.
- **Bounded** — a well-scoped change to code that already exists in
  this repo: a new flag, a small endpoint, a one-file fix.
  Understanding the kind of app is not enough — bounded means the flow
  you are changing is already here to read. If there is no existing
  flow to change, the task is not bounded. Ask the clarifying
  questions that matter, present a short design IN CHAT (a few
  sentences to a few short paragraphs), and STOP. Implementation
  starts only after your human partner says yes to that design — a
  bounded task's approval is as hard a gate as an architectural
  one. No spec file, no implementation plan document.
- **Architectural** — new projects, new subsystems, changes that
  restructure how components fit together or alter interfaces others
  depend on. Follow the full process: questions, approaches, sectioned
  design, written spec, then the writing-plans skill.

When in doubt between two paths, take the heavier one. The ratchet is
one-way: hidden complexity discovered mid-task upgrades the path —
stop, say so, and step up. Nothing downgrades mid-task.

## Anti-Pattern: "Too Simple To Need Approval"

Every path ends with your human partner approving your intent before
implementation. A todo list, a single-function utility, a config
change — the design may be two sentences in chat, but you MUST present
it and get approval. "Simple" tasks are where unexamined assumptions
cause the most wasted work. What scales with simplicity is the
artifact, never the approval.

## Red Flags

| Thought | Reality |
|---------|---------|
| "This is too simple to need a design" | Simple means a short design, not no design. Two sentences in chat, then approval. |
| "I'll call it bounded and skip the spec" | Reaching for a label to skip work IS the doubt — take the heavier path. |
| "It's bounded and the design is obvious — I'll start while they read it" | The gate is the approval, not the design's length. Present, then stop until you hear yes. |
| "I understand this kind of app, so it's bounded" | Bounded measures the repo, not your familiarity. A new project has no existing flow — it is architectural. |
| "The spike works, so I'll keep the code" | A spike's output is an answer. Keeping the code is a new request — classify it. |
| "It grew, but I'm almost done — no need to re-classify" | Hidden complexity upgrades the path mid-task. Stop and say so. |
| "They approved the spike, so the follow-up change is approved too" | Each task gets its own classification and its own approval. |

## Checklist

Classify first, announce the path, then create a task for each item on
your path and complete them in order.

**Spike:**
1. **Explore project context** — enough to frame the probe
2. **Present question + probe plan** — 2-3 sentences
3. **Get approval** — a nod is enough
4. **Investigate** — as cheaply as correctness allows
5. **Report findings** — a recommendation; label anything built as throwaway

**Bounded:**
1. **Explore project context** — check files, docs, recent commits
2. **Ask clarifying questions** — one at a time, the ones that matter
3. **Present short design in chat** — approach, files touched, testing
4. **Get approval** — STOP and wait for an explicit yes; presenting the design and starting in the same breath is skipping the gate
5. **Implement** — proceed with the normal development workflow (TDD applies); no plan document

**Architectural:**
1. **Explore project context** — check files, docs, recent commits
2. **Offer the visual companion just-in-time** — NOT upfront. The first time a question would genuinely be clearer shown than described, offer it then (its own message); on approval its browser tab opens for you. If no visual question ever arises, never offer it. See the Visual Companion section below.
3. **Ask clarifying questions** — one at a time, understand purpose/constraints/success criteria
4. **Propose 2-3 approaches** — with trade-offs and your recommendation
5. **Present design** — in sections scaled to their complexity, get user approval after each section
6. **Write design doc** — save to `docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md` and commit
7. **Spec self-review** — quick inline check for placeholders, contradictions, ambiguity, scope (see below)
8. **User reviews written spec** — ask user to review the spec file before proceeding
9. **Transition to implementation** — invoke writing-plans skill to create implementation plan

## Process Flow

```dot
digraph brainstorming {
    "Classify: spike / bounded / architectural" [shape=diamond];
    "Present question + probe (2-3 sentences)" [shape=box];
    "Ask clarifying questions (bounded)" [shape=box];
    "Present short design in chat" [shape=box];
    "Human approves?" [shape=diamond];
    "Investigate; report recommendation" [shape=doublecircle];
    "Implement via normal workflow (no plan doc)" [shape=doublecircle];
    "Explore project context" [shape=box];
    "Ask clarifying questions" [shape=box];
    "Propose 2-3 approaches" [shape=box];
    "Present design sections" [shape=box];
    "User approves design?" [shape=diamond];
    "Write design doc" [shape=box];
    "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)" [shape=box];
    "User reviews spec?" [shape=diamond];
    "Invoke writing-plans skill" [shape=doublecircle];
    "Hidden complexity? Upgrade path" [shape=box];

    "Classify: spike / bounded / architectural" -> "Present question + probe (2-3 sentences)" [label="spike"];
    "Classify: spike / bounded / architectural" -> "Ask clarifying questions (bounded)" [label="bounded"];
    "Classify: spike / bounded / architectural" -> "Explore project context" [label="architectural"];
    "Present question + probe (2-3 sentences)" -> "Human approves?";
    "Ask clarifying questions (bounded)" -> "Present short design in chat";
    "Present short design in chat" -> "Human approves?";
    "Human approves?" -> "Investigate; report recommendation" [label="spike: yes"];
    "Human approves?" -> "Implement via normal workflow (no plan doc)" [label="bounded: yes"];
    "Hidden complexity? Upgrade path" -> "Classify: spike / bounded / architectural";
    "Explore project context" -> "Ask clarifying questions";
    "Ask clarifying questions" -> "Propose 2-3 approaches";
    "Propose 2-3 approaches" -> "Present design sections";
    "Present design sections" -> "User approves design?";
    "User approves design?" -> "Present design sections" [label="no, revise"];
    "User approves design?" -> "Write design doc" [label="yes"];
    "Write design doc" -> "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)";
    "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)" -> "User reviews spec?";
    "User reviews spec?" -> "Write design doc" [label="changes requested"];
    "User reviews spec?" -> "Invoke writing-plans skill" [label="approved"];
}
```

**Terminal states are path-bound.** Architectural: the ONLY skill you
invoke after brainstorming is writing-plans — never frontend-design,
mcp-builder, or any other implementation skill. Bounded: after
approval, implementation proceeds directly through the normal
development workflow; no plan document. Spike: the terminal state is a
reported recommendation.

## The Process

The subsections below serve the bounded and architectural paths (a
spike stops at "present the probe, get a nod"). Sections from
**Exploring approaches** onward are architectural-path depth — for
bounded work, context plus a few questions plus a short in-chat design
is the whole process.

**Understanding the idea:**

- Check out the current project state first (files, docs, recent commits)
- Before asking detailed questions, assess scope: if the request describes multiple independent subsystems (e.g., "build a platform with chat, file storage, billing, and analytics"), flag this immediately. Don't spend questions refining details of a project that needs to be decomposed first.
- If the project is too large for a single spec, help the user decompose into sub-projects: what are the independent pieces, how do they relate, what order should they be built? Then brainstorm the first sub-project through the normal design flow. Each sub-project gets its own spec → plan → implementation cycle.
- For appropriately-scoped projects, ask questions one at a time to refine the idea
- Prefer multiple choice questions when possible, but open-ended is fine too
- Only one question per message - if a topic needs more exploration, break it into multiple questions
- Focus on understanding: purpose, constraints, success criteria

**Exploring approaches:**

- Propose 2-3 different approaches with trade-offs
- Present options conversationally with your recommendation and reasoning
- Lead with your recommended option and explain why
- YAGNI ruthlessly - remove unnecessary features from every approach and design

**Presenting the design:**

- Once you believe you understand what you're building, present the design
- Scale each section to its complexity: a few sentences if straightforward, up to 200-300 words if nuanced
- Ask after each section whether it looks right so far
- Cover: architecture, components, data flow, error handling, testing
- Be ready to go back and clarify if something doesn't make sense

**Design for isolation and clarity:**

- Break the system into smaller units that each have one clear purpose, communicate through well-defined interfaces, and can be understood and tested independently
- For each unit, you should be able to answer: what does it do, how do you use it, and what does it depend on?
- Can someone understand what a unit does without reading its internals? Can you change the internals without breaking consumers? If not, the boundaries need work.
- Smaller, well-bounded units are also easier for you to work with - you reason better about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. When a file grows large, that's often a signal that it's doing too much.

**Working in existing codebases:**

- Explore the current structure before proposing changes. Follow existing patterns.
- Where existing code has problems that affect the work (e.g., a file that's grown too large, unclear boundaries, tangled responsibilities), include targeted improvements as part of the design - the way a good developer improves code they're working in.
- Don't propose unrelated refactoring. Stay focused on what serves the current goal.

## After the Design (architectural path)

**Documentation:**

- Write the validated design (spec) to `docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`
  - (User preferences for spec location override this default)
- Use elements-of-style:writing-clearly-and-concisely skill if available
- Commit the design document to git

**Spec Self-Review:**
After writing the spec document, look at it with fresh eyes:

1. **Placeholder scan:** Any "TBD", "TODO", incomplete sections, or vague requirements? Fix them.
2. **Internal consistency:** Do any sections contradict each other? Does the architecture match the feature descriptions?
3. **Scope check:** Is this focused enough for a single implementation plan, or does it need decomposition?
4. **Ambiguity check:** Could any requirement be interpreted two different ways? If so, pick one and make it explicit.

Fix any issues inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on.

**User Review Gate:**
After the spec review loop passes, ask the user to review the written spec before proceeding:

> "Spec written and committed to `<path>`. Please review it and let me know if you want to make any changes before we start writing out the implementation plan."

Wait for the user's response. If they request changes, make them and re-run the spec review loop. Only proceed once the user approves.

**Implementation:**

- Invoke the writing-plans skill to create a detailed implementation plan
- Do NOT invoke any other skill. writing-plans is the next step.

## Visual Companion

A browser-based companion for showing mockups, diagrams, and visual options during brainstorming. Available as a tool — not a mode. Accepting the companion means it's available for questions that benefit from visual treatment; it does NOT mean every question goes through the browser.

**Offering the companion (just-in-time):** Do NOT offer it upfront. Wait until a question would genuinely be clearer shown than told — a real mockup / layout / diagram question, not merely a UI *topic*. The first time that happens, offer it then, as its own message:
> "This next part might be easier if I show you — I can put together mockups, diagrams, and comparisons in a browser tab as we go. It's still new and can be token-intensive. Want me to? I'll open it for you."

**This offer MUST be its own message.** Only the offer — no clarifying question, summary, or other content. Wait for the user's response. If they accept, start the server with `--open` so their browser opens to the first screen automatically. If they decline, continue text-only and don't offer again unless they raise it.

**Per-question decision:** Even after the user accepts, decide FOR EACH QUESTION whether to use the browser or the terminal. The test: **would the user understand this better by seeing it than reading it?**

- **Use the browser** for content that IS visual — mockups, wireframes, layout comparisons, architecture diagrams, side-by-side visual designs
- **Use the terminal** for content that is text — requirements questions, conceptual choices, tradeoff lists, A/B/C/D text options, scope decisions

A question about a UI topic is not automatically a visual question. "What does personality mean in this context?" is a conceptual question — use the terminal. "Which wizard layout works better?" is a visual question — use the browser.

If they agree to the companion, read the detailed guide before proceeding:
`skills/brainstorming/visual-companion.md`

questions.question: Which database setup for Prisma persistence?

options.label: PostgreSQL + docker-compose (Recommended)
options.description: Production-like, matches 'SQL persistence' spec strongly, reviewer runs `docker compose up -d` then seed. Also makes the Docker bonus half-done.

options.label: SQLite
options.description: Zero setup for reviewer, but weaker signal for a backend take-home and no full-text search support worth showing.

options.label: PostgreSQL local install
options.description: No Docker dependency, but reviewer setup friction — they need Postgres running with matching credentials.

questions.question: Which CI platform for the build+check bonus and where does the repo live?

options.label: GitHub + GitHub Actions (Recommended)
options.description: Standard for candidate take-homes; reviewers expect it. Workflow: install, lint, typecheck, test, build on every push.

options.label: GitLab + GitLab CI
options.description: You have GitLab tooling connected, but check the assignment — if submission is via GitHub link, Actions is the safer bet.

options.label: Local git only, no CI
options.description: Skip the CI bonus, commit history still graded. Fastest but drops lightly-weighted points.

questions.question: Share-by-token conflicts with 'OIDC on every route' — a public share link means one unauthenticated route. How to resolve? (This becomes a DECISIONS.md ADR either way.)

options.label: Public read-only token route (Recommended)
options.description: GET /shared/:token needs no login — capability URL, read-only, revocable. One documented exception to the OIDC rule, justified in ADR + README. Best sharing UX.

options.label: Signed-in users only
options.description: Recipient must log in; token grants read access to their account. Keeps 'OIDC on every route' literally true, but recipient needs an account — weaker share UX.

options.label: Backend only, no FE share page
options.description: Implement share token issue/revoke + read endpoint, document it, skip the frontend viewer page. Least work, still answers §3.3.

questions.question: Which optional bonuses to include? (§3.1–3.3 solid comes first regardless.)

options.label: Dockerfile (backend + frontend)
options.description: Containerize both; docker-compose already runs the DB so this rounds out one-command startup.

options.label: CI/CD pipeline
options.description: Build + lint + test on every push. Pairs with CI platform choice above.

options.label: /all page
options.description: Collections with bookmarks nested inside — cheap once GET /collections/:id/bookmarks exists.

options.label: Full-text search
options.description: Postgres tsvector across bookmark title + notes, exposed as ?q= filter + FE search box.

Greenfield monorepo at /Users/REDACTED/Desktop/chun/bbl (currently EMPTY, not yet a git repo). Structure will be: /backend (NestJS + TypeScript), /frontend (React+Vite), plus graded docs (CLAUDE.md, API_DESIGN.md, DECISIONS.md, AI_WORKFLOW.md, README.md, /.agent/, /transcripts/).

- NestJS + TypeScript backend, OIDC authentication on EVERY route.
- Auth0: discovery https://AUTH0_DOMAIN_REDACTED/.well-known/openid-configuration, SPA clientId AUTH0_CLIENT_ID_REDACTED, callback http://localhost:3000/callback (FRONTEND route — backend must NOT implement a /callback endpoint), scope "openid profile email", API audience AUTH0_AUDIENCE_REDACTED. Test user EMAIL_REDACTED / TEST_PASSWORD_REDACTED.
- API validates the ACCESS TOKEN (RS256, JWKS from discovery, audience + issuer checks) — NOT the ID token.
- Resources /collections and /bookmarks, each with: get one, list, create, update (PUT), patch (PATCH), delete, and filtering on list. Plus GET /me returning current signed-in user. Plus GET /collections/:id/bookmarks.

Suggested schema (we may refine, must justify changes): Collection {id, name, ownerId, createdAt, updatedAt}; Bookmark {id, url, title, notes?, collectionId?, ownerId, createdAt, updatedAt}. Bookmark belongs-to Collection (nullable = uncategorised); both belong to a user.

1. PostgreSQL via docker-compose.
2. Sharing (§3.3 "A user may want to share a collection with someone else"): SIGNED-IN USERS ONLY — owner issues a share token/invite for a collection; recipient must be authenticated; grants READ-ONLY access. No public unauthenticated route ("OIDC on every route" stays literally true). Documented in README + DECISIONS.md.

Propose a concrete strategy (e.g. seed two users with fake subs like "auth0|seed-user-1", and link the real Auth0 account on first login via email match upsert — or an alternative you justify).
- Don't pin guessed package versions. Say "install latest, verify at implementation time via npm view".

1. Module/folder layout for /backend (NestJS modules: auth, users, collections, bookmarks, shares, prisma, health?).
2. Auth design: global guard (APP_GUARD) with passport-jwt + jwks-rsa vs jose — pick one, justify; where issuer/audience config lives; request.user shape; decorator for current user.
3. Prisma schema: full models (User, Collection, Bookmark, CollectionShare or similar), relations, onDelete behaviors, indexes (incl. tsvector/FTS approach for Postgres — raw migration with tsvector+GIN vs Prisma fullTextSearch preview feature — pick one, justify).
4. API contract sketch: routes, verbs, status codes, list/filter/pagination params (pick page-based or cursor, justify), error envelope shape, validation approach (class-validator DTOs vs zod — pick, justify for NestJS).
5. Share feature design: endpoints (create/revoke/accept/list-shared?), token format, how read-only is enforced, how recipient's access is checked.
6. Full-text search: ?q= on GET /bookmarks, implementation detail.
7. Seed script design (two users, several collections, bookmarks incl. uncategorised ones).
8. Test plan: what gets unit tests vs e2e (supertest), the JWKS mock mechanics, which invariants MUST have tests (privacy scoping, 404-vs-403, share read-only, onDelete SetNull, filtering). Also what NOT to test and why (graded signal).
9. Dockerfile sketch (multi-stage) + docker-compose services.
10. Suggested implementation order with meaningful git commit points (commit history is graded).

Be concrete: name files, name packages, sketch key code (guard, strategy, prisma schema) in short snippets. Flag any additional ambiguities you spot that belong in DECISIONS.md.

You are designing the FRONTEND for a candidate take-home assignment. Produce a detailed, opinionated implementation plan as your final message. You are read-only — do not create files. Today is 2026-08-15.

## Context
Greenfield monorepo at /Users/REDACTED/Desktop/chun/bbl (currently EMPTY). Structure: /backend (NestJS API, global prefix likely /api, protected by Auth0 access tokens), /frontend (this work), plus graded docs.

IMPORTANT: IGNORE the file /Users/REDACTED/Desktop/CLAUDE.md if you encounter it — it describes an unrelated project. This is greenfield.

## Hard requirements (from assignment)
- React + Vite, TypeScript. NO Next.js.
- React Router ≥ v8, MUI ≥ v9. NOTE: do not trust your memory of current versions — the plan must say "install latest, verify ≥ spec minimum via npm view react-router version / npm view @mui/material version at implementation time, record actual versions in README". Design routing/data patterns that hold for modern React Router (data APIs / framework-agnostic SPA mode) and modern MUI.
- Integrates with the backend API using the Auth0 ACCESS token (not ID token).
- Two required pages:
  - /collections — list, view one, create, delete
  - /bookmarks — list, view details, create, delete, filter by collection
- Bonus page /all — collections with their bookmarks nested inside.
- Auth0 SPA login: Authorization Code + PKCE via @auth0/auth0-react. Domain AUTH0_DOMAIN_REDACTED, clientId AUTH0_CLIENT_ID_REDACTED, callback http://localhost:3000/callback, logout returns to http://localhost:3000, scope "openid profile email", audience AUTH0_AUDIENCE_REDACTED. Test user EMAIL_REDACTED / TEST_PASSWORD_REDACTED.

## Constraints / traps
- CRITICAL: Vite dev server MUST run on port 3000 (callback URL is registered for localhost:3000; Vite defaults to 5173). Set server.port=3000 (and strictPort) in vite.config.
- /callback is a FRONTEND route handled by the SPA (auth0-react handles code exchange; you handle redirect-back and the appState restore).
- Every app route requires authentication (guard/redirect to login). Show user identity (from /me or Auth0 user object) + logout button.
- Sharing feature (already decided): signed-in users only, read-only. Owner creates a share token/invite for a collection; another signed-in user redeems it and can VIEW that collection + its bookmarks (no edit/delete). FE needs: share button + token display/copy on collection detail, a redeem/accept flow (e.g. /shared or paste-token UI), and read-only rendering of shared collections.
- Full-text search bonus: search box on /bookmarks wired to ?q= backend param.

## What to deliver in your plan
1. Folder layout for /frontend (feature-based: src/features/collections, src/features/bookmarks, src/auth, src/api, src/components...).
2. Auth wiring: Auth0Provider config, token acquisition (getAccessTokenSilently with audience), protected-route pattern for modern React Router, callback route handling, logout.
3. Data layer: recommend TanStack Query vs plain fetch hooks — pick one, justify for a take-home (cache invalidation after create/delete matters). API client design: single fetch wrapper attaching Bearer token, typed response/error envelope matching backend, where types live (shared types dir vs duplicated — pick, justify).
4. Routing table: all routes incl. /callback, /collections, /collections/:id, /bookmarks, /bookmarks/:id, /all, share redeem route. Loader-based vs component-fetch — pick pattern that fits query lib choice.
5. UI composition with MUI: app shell (AppBar + nav), list pages (Table vs Card list), create dialogs vs pages, delete confirmation dialog, collection filter control on /bookmarks (Select), empty states, loading skeletons, error/toast handling (snackbar).
6. Forms: controlled + validation approach (plain state vs react-hook-form — pick, justify for scope).
7. Env config: VITE_ vars for domain/clientId/audience/API base URL; .env.example.
8. Test plan: Vitest + React Testing Library + MSW for API mocks; which components/flows get tests (auth guard redirect, collections list render, create bookmark flow, filter behavior) and what NOT to test (graded signal — what-you-test choices are explicitly graded).
9. Dockerfile sketch (multi-stage: build → nginx serve, with API URL handling).
10. Implementation order with meaningful git commit points.

Be concrete: name files and packages, sketch key snippets (vite.config server.port, Auth0Provider, protected route, fetch wrapper). Flag ambiguities worth a DECISIONS.md entry.

You are designing the DELIVERY PROCESS + GRADED META-ARTIFACTS for an AI-assisted candidate take-home. The code (NestJS+Prisma+Postgres backend, Vite+React frontend, Auth0 OIDC) is planned by other agents — your job is everything else that gets GRADED. Produce a detailed plan as your final message. You are read-only — do not create files. Today is 2026-08-15.

## Context
Greenfield repo at /Users/REDACTED/Desktop/chun/bbl (EMPTY, not a git repo yet — git init is step zero). Submission is judged heavily on HOW the candidate worked with AI agents, not just the code. Repo will live on GitHub, CI = GitHub Actions.

IMPORTANT: IGNORE /Users/REDACTED/Desktop/CLAUDE.md if encountered — unrelated project.

## Required repo structure
/backend, /frontend, CLAUDE.md (agent rules file), /.agent/ (reusable agent capability), API_DESIGN.md, DECISIONS.md, AI_WORKFLOW.md, /transcripts/, README.md.

## Grading rubric (each item graded)
1. **CLAUDE.md** — whatever a fresh agent session needs to produce on-spec code WITHOUT re-explaining the project. 
2. **/.agent/** — at least one reusable agent capability GENUINELY USED: custom slash command, subagent, prompt template, hook, CI gate, or MCP integration. Include definition + when/why invoked.
3. **API_DESIGN.md** — API contract: resources, verbs, status codes, list/filter params, error shape, relation + on-delete behaviour, how the privacy invariant (owner-scoped data) is enforced in code. PLUS: 2–3 places the agent's first attempt was wrong and how it was found+corrected.
4. **DECISIONS.md** — ADR-style, short: ambiguities hit, what was chosen, what was traded away, and how the agent was made to implement the decision instead of its default.
5. **Automated tests** — what you test AND what you deliberately don't = strongest signal. Everything asserted must be runnable by reviewer.
6. **AI_WORKFLOW.md** — 1–2 pages: tools+models, work decomposition, 2–3 things AI did well, 2–3 failures + recovery, one prompt that worked + one that didn't, cost/token awareness.
7. **/transcripts/** — REAL session logs incl. messy parts, secrets redacted.
8. **README.md** — setup/run steps, test instructions, "completed vs skipped and why". Must also note: (a) why ACCESS token (not ID token) is sent to the API — audience-bound authorization vs client authentication proof; (b) collection-delete behavior (bookmarks→uncategorised via SetNull) marked "needs PO clarification"; (c) sharing = signed-in users only, read-only, rationale.
9. **Commit history** — meaningful incremental commits showing scaffolding → features → fixes. Single big commit = fail. Messy honest history beats clean single commit.

## Known decisions (context for ADRs)
Postgres+docker-compose; GitHub Actions; share=signed-in-only read-only via share token; delete collection→SetNull+PO note; 404 not 403 cross-user; all 4 bonuses (Dockerfile BE+FE, CI, /all page, Postgres FTS); access-token-not-id-token; /me via /userinfo upsert (no Auth0 tenant admin → no custom claims); tests never hit live Auth0 (locally-signed RS256 + mocked JWKS); seed 2 fake-sub users + email-match link for real test user.

## What to deliver in your plan
1. **Git/commit strategy**: concrete commit sequence mapped to build phases (init+docs skeleton → BE scaffold → auth guard+/me → prisma schema+seed → collections CRUD → bookmarks CRUD+filters → nested route → shares → FE scaffold+auth → FE pages → tests → docs → bonuses). Commit message convention (conventional commits?). When to commit doc updates (interleaved, not one dump at end).
2. **CLAUDE.md outline** for THIS repo: stack, commands, port-3000 constraint, auth model, privacy invariant, error envelope, test commands, "never hit live Auth0 in tests", DECISIONS.md is authoritative over agent defaults, etc.
3. **/.agent/ capability recommendation**: pick 1–2 that are genuinely useful DURING this build and honest to document. Candidates: (a) /api-contract-check slash command — reads API_DESIGN.md, greps controllers/DTOs, reports drift; (b) pre-commit or CI gate running lint+test; (c) a code-review subagent pass before each commit. Recommend + give the actual definition file content sketch.
4. **API_DESIGN.md skeleton**: section list. Plus PROCESS design: how to capture "agent's first attempt was wrong" moments IN REAL TIME (they can't be reconstructed later) — e.g. a running WORKLOG or DECISIONS scratch file updated at each correction.
5. **DECISIONS.md**: enumerate the expected ADR list now (share semantics; delete behavior; 404-vs-403; pagination style; user provisioning//me //userinfo; test-auth mock strategy; monorepo tooling — recommend npm workspaces vs plain dirs, pick one; FTS implementation; PUT-vs-PATCH semantics; error envelope). ADR template (Context/Decision/Trade-off/How-agent-was-steered).
6. **AI_WORKFLOW.md skeleton** + real-time capture habit.
7. **/transcripts/ mechanics**: Claude Code session JSONL lives under ~/.claude/projects/<encoded-cwd>/ — plan: copy+redact at milestones (redact tokens, no secrets; Auth0 client id is public-ish for SPA but redact anyway?Decide). Also markdown-exported summaries per session.
8. **README.md skeleton** incl. quickstart (docker compose up, prisma migrate+seed, two terminals or one root script), test-run section, completed-vs-skipped table.
9. **GitHub Actions workflow design**: jobs (backend: lint+typecheck+test with Postgres service container? or mocked-DB unit tests only — decide; frontend: lint+typecheck+test+build), triggers, node version, cache.
10. **Monorepo tooling call**: npm workspaces + root scripts (concurrently) vs two independent packages — recommend one, justify.

Be concrete and terse. Output: numbered plan with file content sketches where valuable.

# Backend Implementation Plan — Bookmarks/Collections API (NestJS + Prisma + Auth0)

Target: `/Users/REDACTED/Desktop/chun/bbl/backend`. All paths below are relative to that unless absolute.

## 1. Module / folder layout

```
/backend
├── Dockerfile
├── .env.example                  # AUTH0_ISSUER, AUTH0_AUDIENCE, AUTH0_JWKS_URI, DATABASE_URL, PORT
├── package.json                  # install latest of everything; verify via `npm view <pkg> version` at impl time
├── prisma/
│   ├── schema.prisma
│   ├── migrations/               # incl. hand-edited FTS migration (see §3)
│   └── seed.ts
├── src/
│   ├── main.ts                   # global ValidationPipe, port 3001 (FE owns 3000)
│   ├── app.module.ts             # ConfigModule.forRoot({validate}), APP_GUARD registration
│   ├── config/
│   │   └── env.validation.ts     # class-validator on process.env; fail fast on boot
│   ├── prisma/
│   │   ├── prisma.module.ts      # @Global()
│   │   └── prisma.service.ts     # extends PrismaClient, onModuleInit/$connect
│   ├── auth/
│   │   ├── auth.module.ts
│   │   ├── jwt.strategy.ts       # RS256 + JWKS + issuer/audience checks
│   │   ├── jwt-auth.guard.ts     # extends AuthGuard('jwt'); NO bypass logic
│   │   ├── current-user.decorator.ts
│   │   ├── auth-user.interface.ts  # { userId; sub; email }
│   │   └── userinfo.client.ts    # thin fetch wrapper over Auth0 /userinfo
│   ├── users/
│   │   ├── users.module.ts
│   │   ├── users.service.ts      # resolveFromToken(): cache → DB → /userinfo upsert
│   │   └── me.controller.ts      # GET /me
│   ├── collections/              # controller, service, dto/ (create, update=PartialType, query)
│   ├── bookmarks/                # controller, service, dto/, search via $queryRaw
│   ├── shares/                   # controller, service, dto/
│   └── common/
│       ├── dto/pagination.dto.ts # page, limit with defaults/caps
│       └── interfaces/paginated.interface.ts
└── test/
    ├── jest-e2e.json
    ├── utils/test-auth.ts        # local keypair, JWKS nock, signToken()
    ├── utils/test-db.ts          # truncate helpers
    ├── auth.e2e-spec.ts
    ├── me.e2e-spec.ts
    ├── collections.e2e-spec.ts
    ├── bookmarks.e2e-spec.ts
    ├── search.e2e-spec.ts
    └── shares.e2e-spec.ts
```

**Deliberately absent: a health module.** With "OIDC on every route" taken literally (decision #2's rationale), a public `/health` would break the invariant and an authenticated one is useless to orchestrators. Liveness comes from the container level: `pg_isready` healthcheck on the db service, and Docker's process supervision for the API. Record this in DECISIONS.md — it is exactly the kind of trade-off graders look for.

Packages (all "install latest, verify with `npm view` at implementation time"): `@nestjs/{core,common,platform-express,config,passport}`, `passport`, `passport-jwt`, `jwks-rsa`, `@prisma/client` + `prisma`, `class-validator`, `class-transformer`. Dev: `jest`, `supertest`, `nock`, `jose` (test-only, for signing), `ts-jest`, `eslint`, `prettier`.

## 2. Auth design

**Pick: `passport-jwt` + `jwks-rsa`, global `APP_GUARD`.** Rationale over `jose`:
- Idiomatic NestJS (`@nestjs/passport`) — graders recognize it instantly.
- `jwks-rsa`'s `passportJwtSecret` gives JWKS caching + rate limiting for free.
- **The decisive one:** `jwks-rsa` fetches JWKS over Node's classic http stack, which `nock` intercepts. `jose`'s `createRemoteJWKSet` uses undici `fetch`, which nock does not reliably intercept — that would undermine the "tests never touch live Auth0" mechanism, our top graded signal.

Config lives in `.env` / `env.validation.ts`:

```
AUTH0_ISSUER=https://AUTH0_DOMAIN_REDACTED/        # TRAILING SLASH — Auth0 mints iss with it; classic 401 bug
AUTH0_AUDIENCE=AUTH0_AUDIENCE_REDACTED
AUTH0_JWKS_URI=https://AUTH0_DOMAIN_REDACTED/.well-known/jwks.json
```

Making `AUTH0_JWKS_URI` its own variable (not derived) is what lets e2e tests point it at a nocked URL without touching strategy code.

```ts
// src/auth/jwt.strategy.ts
@Injectable()
export class JwtStrategy extends PassportStrategy(Strategy, 'jwt') {
  constructor(config: ConfigService, private readonly users: UsersService) {
    super({
      jwtFromRequest: ExtractJwt.fromAuthHeaderAsBearerToken(),
      algorithms: ['RS256'],
      issuer: config.getOrThrow('AUTH0_ISSUER'),
      audience: config.getOrThrow('AUTH0_AUDIENCE'),
      secretOrKeyProvider: passportJwtSecret({
        cache: true,
        rateLimit: true,
        jwksRequestsPerMinute: 5,
        jwksUri: config.getOrThrow('AUTH0_JWKS_URI'),
      }),
      passReqToCallback: true, // need the raw bearer to call /userinfo on first sight of a sub
    });
  }

  async validate(req: Request, payload: { sub: string }): Promise<AuthUser> {
    const accessToken = ExtractJwt.fromAuthHeaderAsBearerToken()(req)!;
    return this.users.resolveFromToken(payload.sub, accessToken);
  }
}
```

```ts
// app.module.ts providers
{ provide: APP_GUARD, useClass: JwtAuthGuard }
```

`JwtAuthGuard` is a bare `extends AuthGuard('jwt')` — **no `@Public()` decorator exists in the codebase.** "OIDC on every route" is then true by construction; there is no mechanism for an accidentally public endpoint. This is worth a line in DECISIONS.md.

**`request.user` shape:** `{ userId: string; sub: string; email: string }` — `userId` is the *internal* DB id; all query scoping uses it, never the raw sub. `@CurrentUser()` is a one-line `createParamDecorator` returning `req.user`.

**`/me` and user provisioning** (solves the "access token carries no email" trap — with `audience` set, Auth0 issues a plain access token with only `sub`):

`UsersService.resolveFromToken(sub, accessToken)`:
1. In-memory `Map<sub, AuthUser>` cache hit → return (zero DB/network cost per request).
2. DB `findUnique({ where: { sub } })` hit → cache, return.
3. Miss → call `GET {AUTH0_ISSUER}userinfo` with the bearer (scope `openid profile email` covers it) → get `{ sub, email, name }` → **upsert keyed by email**: if a seed row with that email exists, update its `sub` to the real Auth0 sub (this is the seed-linkage mechanism, §7); else create. Cache, return.

Consequence: `/userinfo` is hit **once per unknown sub per process lifetime**, never per request. Auth0 rate-limits `/userinfo` aggressively (~5 req/min/user) — cite this in DECISIONS.md as the justification. `GET /me` itself just returns the local User row from `req.user.userId`.

## 3. Prisma schema

```prisma
// prisma/schema.prisma
model User {
  id             String            @id @default(cuid())
  sub            String            @unique
  email          String            @unique
  name           String?
  createdAt      DateTime          @default(now())
  updatedAt      DateTime          @updatedAt
  collections    Collection[]
  bookmarks      Bookmark[]
  sharesReceived CollectionShare[] @relation("ShareGrantee")
}

model Collection {
  id        String            @id @default(cuid())
  name      String
  ownerId   String
  owner     User              @relation(fields: [ownerId], references: [id], onDelete: Cascade)
  bookmarks Bookmark[]
  shares    CollectionShare[]
  createdAt DateTime          @default(now())
  updatedAt DateTime          @updatedAt
  @@index([ownerId])
}

model Bookmark {
  id           String               @id @default(cuid())
  url          String
  title        String
  notes        String?
  collectionId String?
  collection   Collection?          @relation(fields: [collectionId], references: [id], onDelete: SetNull)
  ownerId      String
  owner        User                 @relation(fields: [ownerId], references: [id], onDelete: Cascade)
  searchVector Unsupported("tsvector")?   // managed by raw SQL in migration; keeps prisma migrate diff honest
  createdAt    DateTime             @default(now())
  updatedAt    DateTime             @updatedAt
  @@index([ownerId])
  @@index([collectionId])
}

model CollectionShare {
  id            String     @id @default(cuid())
  collectionId  String
  collection    Collection @relation(fields: [collectionId], references: [id], onDelete: Cascade)
  token         String     @unique
  granteeUserId String?
  grantee       User?      @relation("ShareGrantee", fields: [granteeUserId], references: [id], onDelete: Cascade)
  createdAt     DateTime   @default(now())
  revokedAt     DateTime?
  @@unique([collectionId, granteeUserId])
  @@index([granteeUserId])
}
```

Deviations from the suggested schema — justify in DECISIONS.md:
- **Added `User` model.** Required for `/me`, referential integrity on `ownerId`, and the seed-linkage strategy. Internal cuid PK with `sub @unique` rather than sub-as-PK: first-login linking rewrites the sub of a seeded user; with an internal PK that is a one-column update and every FK (`ownerId`, `granteeUserId`) stays stable. Sub-as-PK would force cascading key updates.
- **Added `CollectionShare`** for decision #2 (sharing).
- `email @unique` — the linchpin of email-match linking.
- `onDelete: SetNull` on `Bookmark.collection` implements decision #3 exactly; `Cascade` on owner relations (user deletion isn't exposed via API, but integrity should hold).

**FTS: raw migration with generated tsvector + GIN — not Prisma's `fullTextSearch` preview.** Justification: the preview flag's API has changed across Prisma majors (`search:` arg shape, `previewFeatures` naming) and offers no control over index type or ranking; a generated column is version-proof, indexes properly, and demonstrates SQL competence. Mechanics: `npx prisma migrate dev --create-only`, then append to the generated SQL:

```sql
ALTER TABLE "Bookmark" ADD COLUMN "searchVector" tsvector
  GENERATED ALWAYS AS (
    to_tsvector('english', coalesce("title", '') || ' ' || coalesce("notes", ''))
  ) STORED;
CREATE INDEX "Bookmark_searchVector_idx" ON "Bookmark" USING GIN ("searchVector");
```

The `Unsupported("tsvector")?` field in the model prevents `migrate dev` from trying to drop the column later.

## 4. API contract sketch

All routes require `Authorization: Bearer <access token>`; there are no exceptions.

| Route | Verb | Success | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `/me` | GET | 200 | Local user row `{id, sub, email, name, createdAt}` |
| `/collections` | GET | 200 | Filters: `?name=` (contains, case-insensitive); paginated |
| `/collections` | POST | 201 | |
| `/collections/:id` | GET | 200 | Owner OR active grantee |
| `/collections/:id` | PUT | 200 | Full replace; owner only |
| `/collections/:id` | PATCH | 200 | Partial; owner only |
| `/collections/:id` | DELETE | 204 | Owner only; bookmarks → `collectionId = NULL` |
| `/collections/:id/bookmarks` | GET | 200 | Owner OR grantee; paginated |
| `/collections/shared-with-me` | GET | 200 | Collections where I'm an active grantee (route declared BEFORE `/collections/:id` to avoid shadowing) |
| `/bookmarks` | GET | 200 | Filters: `?q=` (FTS), `?collectionId=`, `?uncategorised=true` (collectionId IS NULL); paginated. Powers the `/all` bonus page |
| `/bookmarks` | POST | 201 | `collectionId`, if given, must resolve to an **owned** collection else 404 |
| `/bookmarks/:id` | GET/PUT/PATCH/DELETE | 200/200/200/204 | Owner only |
| `/collections/:id/shares` | POST | 201 | Owner mints invite; response includes `token` (only time it's shown) |
| `/shares` | GET | 200 | Shares I have issued (with accepted/revoked state) |
| `/shares/:id` | DELETE | 204 | Owner revokes (sets `revokedAt`) |
| `/shares/accept` | POST | 200 | Body `{token}`; binds `granteeUserId` = me |

**Errors:** 400 validation, 401 missing/expired/wrong-aud/wrong-iss token, **404 for both nonexistent and cross-user resources** (decision #4 — one code path: scoped `findFirst` returns null → `NotFoundException`, so leaking via a distinguishable 403 is structurally impossible), 409 for share-token conflicts. **Envelope: keep Nest's default `{statusCode, message, error}`** and document it in API_DESIGN.md — a custom envelope adds surface without signal; note this as a deliberate choice in DECISIONS.md.

**Pagination: page-based** — `?page=1&limit=20` (max 100), response `{ data: [...], meta: { page, limit, total, totalPages } }`. Justification: bookmark counts are small, the FE needs "page X of Y" trivially, and cursor pagination's consistency benefits only pay off at scale/infinite-scroll. Cursor noted as rejected alternative in DECISIONS.md.

**Validation: class-validator + class-transformer DTOs**, global `ValidationPipe({ whitelist: true, forbidNonWhitelisted: true, transform: true })`. Rationale over zod: it is the native NestJS mechanism, integrates with `PartialType` for zero-duplication PATCH DTOs, and needs no custom pipe plumbing. PUT reuses `CreateXDto` (full representation required; omitted optional fields like `notes` are set to `null` — document this PUT semantic in API_DESIGN.md). PATCH uses `PartialType(CreateXDto)`. `url` validated with `@IsUrl({ require_protocol: true })`.

## 5. Share feature design

- **Token:** `crypto.randomBytes(32).toString('base64url')`, stored raw with `@unique`. (Hashing-at-rest noted in DECISIONS.md as production hardening deliberately skipped — the token grants read-only access to bookmark lists, and the DB is local.)
- **Flow:** owner `POST /collections/:id/shares` → `{ id, token, ... }` → token conveyed out-of-band → recipient (authenticated — decision #2) `POST /shares/accept { token }` → server checks token exists, `revokedAt IS NULL`, `granteeUserId IS NULL` (single-use invite), grantee ≠ owner (400), then sets `granteeUserId`. Re-accepting by the same user is idempotent-200; a second different user gets 409. Single-use-invite vs multi-use-link is an ambiguity → DECISIONS.md.
- **Read-only enforcement is structural, not conditional:** two query shapes in `CollectionsService`:

```ts
// READ paths (GET /collections/:id, GET /collections/:id/bookmarks)
where: { id, OR: [
  { ownerId: userId },
  { shares: { some: { granteeUserId: userId, revokedAt: null } } },
]}

// WRITE paths (PUT/PATCH/DELETE) — owner only, so a grantee's write finds nothing → 404
where: { id, ownerId: userId }
```

  There is no "role check" to forget — writes simply cannot see shared rows, which also satisfies decision #4 (grantee write attempt → 404, not 403).
- **Scope of the grant:** read access to the collection AND its bookmarks (a collection share without its bookmarks is useless). Uncategorised bookmarks are never shared — they belong to no collection. → DECISIONS.md.
- **Revoke:** soft (`revokedAt` timestamp) so `GET /shares` shows history; all access checks filter `revokedAt: null`, so revocation is instant.

## 6. Full-text search (`?q=` on GET /bookmarks)

When `q` is absent: normal Prisma `findMany`. When present, `$queryRaw` with tagged templates (parameterized — no injection):

```ts
const rows = await this.prisma.$queryRaw<BookmarkRow[]>`
  SELECT id, url, title, notes, "collectionId", "ownerId", "createdAt", "updatedAt",
         ts_rank("searchVector", websearch_to_tsquery('english', ${q})) AS rank,
         count(*) OVER() AS total
  FROM "Bookmark"
  WHERE "ownerId" = ${userId}
    AND "searchVector" @@ websearch_to_tsquery('english', ${q})
    ${collectionId ? Prisma.sql`AND "collectionId" = ${collectionId}` : Prisma.empty}
  ORDER BY rank DESC, "createdAt" DESC
  LIMIT ${limit} OFFSET ${(page - 1) * limit}`;
```

- `websearch_to_tsquery` tolerates arbitrary user input (quotes, `-negation`) without throwing, unlike `to_tsquery`.
- `count(*) OVER()` avoids a second round-trip for pagination meta.
- **The `"ownerId" = ${userId}` predicate inside raw SQL is the single most dangerous line in the codebase** — Prisma's implicit scoping doesn't apply here. It gets a dedicated e2e test (§8).

## 7. Seed script (`prisma/seed.ts`, wired via `"prisma": { "seed": "ts-node prisma/seed.ts" }`)

**Linkage strategy (the trap):** the real test user's `sub` is unknowable until first login. So:
- **User 1:** `email: 'EMAIL_REDACTED'`, `sub: 'auth0|seed-candidate'` (placeholder). On the first real login, `resolveFromToken` misses on the real sub, calls `/userinfo`, gets `email: EMAIL_REDACTED`, and the email-keyed upsert **replaces the placeholder sub with the real one — same row id, so every seeded collection/bookmark/share instantly belongs to the live session**.
- **User 2:** `email: 'EMAIL_REDACTED'`, `sub: 'auth0|seed-user-2'` — never logs in; exists purely to prove privacy scoping (their data must never appear).

Data set: user 1 gets 3 collections ("Engineering", "Reading List", "Recipes"), ~8 bookmarks spread across them + 2 uncategorised (`collectionId: null`); user 2 gets 2 collections, 4 bookmarks + 1 uncategorised. Titles/notes seeded with searchable phrases ("PostgreSQL full text search deep dive", "TypeScript strict mode notes") so `?q=` demos well. Also seed **one accepted `CollectionShare`** (user 2's collection → grantee user 1) so "shared with me" is populated on first login — safe because linking preserves user 1's row id. Script is idempotent: `upsert` keyed on `email` / deterministic ids, so `prisma db seed` can rerun.

## 8. Test plan

**JWKS mock mechanics (top graded signal — exact mechanism):**

```ts
// test/utils/test-auth.ts
import { generateKeyPair, exportJWK, SignJWT } from 'jose';
import nock from 'nock';

const ISSUER = 'https://AUTH0_DOMAIN_REDACTED/';       // same values as prod config
const AUDIENCE = 'AUTH0_AUDIENCE_REDACTED';

export async function setupTestAuth() {
  const { publicKey, privateKey } = await generateKeyPair('RS256');
  const jwk = { ...(await exportJWK(publicKey)), kid: 'test-key', alg: 'RS256', use: 'sig' };
  nock('https://AUTH0_DOMAIN_REDACTED')
    .persist()
    .get('/.well-known/jwks.json').reply(200, { keys: [jwk] });
  nock('https://AUTH0_DOMAIN_REDACTED')
    .persist()
    .get('/userinfo').reply(200, function () {  // sub-aware stub for provisioning tests
      /* decode bearer from this.req.headers, return matching {sub, email, name} */
    });
  nock.disableNetConnect();
  nock.enableNetConnect('127.0.0.1');            // supertest still works; live Auth0 is unreachable

  return (claims: { sub: string } & Partial<{ aud: string; iss: string; exp: number }>) =>
    new SignJWT({})
      .setProtectedHeader({ alg: 'RS256', kid: 'test-key' })
      .setIssuer(claims.iss ?? ISSUER)
      .setAudience(claims.aud ?? AUDIENCE)
      .setSubject(claims.sub)
      .setIssuedAt().setExpirationTime(claims.exp ?? '10m')
      .sign(privateKey);
}
```

This exercises the **real** `jwks-rsa` code path — kid lookup, JWKS caching, issuer/audience verification — with zero live traffic; `nock.disableNetConnect()` makes accidental live calls a hard test failure. (Alternative considered: injecting a test `secretOrKeyProvider` — rejected because it bypasses the very JWKS code we need to prove works.) Test DB: dedicated database on the compose Postgres (`DATABASE_URL` override, `migrate deploy` in `globalSetup`, truncate tables between suites).

**E2E (supertest — the primary layer; the graded invariants live here):**
1. **Auth:** no token → 401; expired → 401; wrong `aud` → 401; wrong `iss` (issuer *without* trailing slash — pins the classic bug) → 401; valid → 200.
2. **Privacy scoping:** user A's list endpoints never contain user B's rows; every entity, every list filter.
3. **404-not-403:** user A GET/PUT/PATCH/DELETE on user B's collection and bookmark ids → 404, response body indistinguishable from a random nonexistent id.
4. **Share read-only:** accept flow works; grantee can GET collection + its bookmarks; grantee PUT/PATCH/DELETE on it → 404; grantee POST bookmark with that collectionId → 404; after revoke, GET → 404; non-grantee with a valid collection id → 404.
5. **onDelete SetNull:** create collection + bookmarks, DELETE collection → 204, bookmarks still exist with `collectionId: null` and appear under `?uncategorised=true`.
6. **FTS + scoping in raw SQL:** `?q=` matches title and notes; user B seeds a bookmark with the exact search phrase → user A's `?q=` results MUST NOT contain it (guards the `$queryRaw` predicate).
7. **Provisioning/linking:** token with unknown sub → `/userinfo` nock hit once → user created; token with new sub + seeded email → seed row relinked (same id, new sub), seeded data returned; second request → no `/userinfo` call (cache assertion via nock interceptor counts).
8. **Validation:** unknown body field → 400 (`forbidNonWhitelisted`); malformed URL → 400; `limit=500` clamped/rejected.

**Unit tests (thin, targeted):** `UsersService.resolveFromToken` branch logic (cache/DB/userinfo, mocked Prisma + userinfo client); `SharesService.accept` edge cases (own token, already-claimed, revoked); pagination DTO clamping.

**Deliberately NOT tested (state this in the test README section — it is a graded signal):** live Auth0 integration (prohibited, non-hermetic); Prisma client internals and migration SQL correctness (vendor-tested; the *behavioral outcome* SetNull is e2e-tested instead); NestJS DI/routing plumbing; controller methods as units (pure delegation — e2e covers the contract, unit-testing them would just mock everything and assert mocks); class-validator's own rules (we test *our* DTO config once via 400s, not the library).
